'''Roger Dingledine''' is an American computer scientist who co-founded [[the Tor Project]]. An [[MIT]] graduate in mathematics, computer science, and electrical engineering, Dingledine is also known by the pseudonym '''arma.'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.torproject.org/about/corepeople.html.en#arma|title=Tor Project: Core People|publisher=The Tor Project|access-date=2017-12-16}}</ref> {{As of|2016|12|post=,}} he is Project Leader, Director, and Research Director at the Tor Project.<ref name = TorPeople>{{cite web|url=https://www.torproject.org/about/corepeople.html.en|title=Tor Project: Core People|publisher=The Tor Project}}</ref> 

==Education==
Dingledine graduated from [[MIT]] with [[Bachelor of Science]] degrees in Mathematics and Computer Science and Engineering in 2000. He later obtained a [[Master of Engineering]] in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from [[MIT]].<ref name="cv">{{cite web|url=http://www.freehaven.net/~arma/cv.html|title=Roger Dingledine's Curriculum Vitae|website=freehaven.net|access-date=31 December 2016}}</ref>

==Career==
===Tor Project===
Tor was developed by Dingledine<ref>{{cite web|last=Dingledine|first=Roger|date=2002-06-26|title=Initial revision - svn:r2 - master tor-0.4.6.0-alpha-dev - debian-version-0.0.1+0.0.2pre19-1 - Roger Dingledine committed on Jun 26, 2002 - 1 parent 766a465 commit 9a928eeb1215f0d7c9b6d0bb9e4571d0a16ed79a Showing 67 changed files with 12,287 additions and 0 deletions.|website=[[GitHub]]|url=https://github.com/torproject/tor/commit/9a928eeb12|access-date=2020-12-27}}</ref>—with [[Nick Mathewson]] and [[Paul Syverson]]<ref name="TorPeople" />—under a contract from the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]].<ref name = MITTRinnovU3506>{{cite journal | author = MIT Tech Rev Staff | year = 2006 | title = Innovators Under 35: Roger Dingledine | journal = MIT Technology Review | issue = September/October | format = print and online | url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=583 | access-date=2016-12-31}}</ref>{{As of|2006|post=,}} the software they developed was being distributed using proceeds from the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]], by the [[Tor Project]].<ref name="MITTRinnovU3506" /> As described at the end of 2015,

{{quote|The Tor Project develops and maintains ... The Tor Browser system, also known as The Onion Router ... a free, open source and sophisticated privacy tool that provides anonymity for web surfing and communication}} as well as developing and maintaining other software tools and applications.<ref name=ZetterWired151211>{{cite magazine | author = Zetter, Kim | date = 2015-12-11 | title=Tor Hires a New Leader to Help It Combat the War on Privacy | magazine = Wired | format = print and online | url=https://www.wired.com/2015/12/tor-hires-a-new-leader-to-help-it-combat-the-war-on-privacy/ | access-date = 2016-01-04 }}</ref><ref>As described by the ''MIT Technology Review'' at the time of the launch of the Tor Project, its function at the time was as follows. "To disguise Internet traffic's origins, Tor plots a route through any three of more than 700 volunteer-run Onion routers around the world. It sets up a two-way link between the sender's computer and the final router in the chain; data passed between them is encrypted in three layers, and each router in the chain peels off one layer along the way. Each data packet "remembers" only the address of the last router it visited. That way, even if the data is intercepted before the final router hands it off to the recipient, it's difficult to trace back to the sender." See MIT Tech Rev Staff, 2006, op. cit.</ref>

[[File:Roger Dingledine DEFCON 2023 presentation.jpg|200px|thumb|left|Dingledine at a panel discussion during DEFCON 2023]]

== Publications and presentations ==
Dingledine has written several highly cited papers, including the Tor design paper titled '''Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router''',<ref>{{cite journal|title=Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router|url=https://www.usenix.org/conference/13th-usenix-security-symposium/tor-second-generation-onion-router|first1=Roger|last1=Dingledine|first2=Nick|last2=Mathewson|first3=Paul|last3=Syverson|journal=Proceedings of the 13th USENIX Security Symposium|year=2004}}</ref> which won the Usenix Security "Test of Time" award.<ref>{{cite conference|url=https://www.usenix.org/conferences/test-of-time-awards|title=USENIX Test of Time Awards|access-date=2020-12-28|publisher=USENIX}}</ref>  Other highly cited papers include [[Mixminion]]’s protocols for anonymous email,<ref>{{cite conference|title=Mixminion: Design of a type III anonymous remailer protocol|url=https://git.gnunet.org/bibliography.git/plain/docs/minion-design.pdf|first1=George|last1=Danezis|first2=Roger|last2=Dingledine|first3=Nick|last3=Mathewson|date=2003-05-11|conference=2003 Symposium on Security and Privacy|pages=2–15|publisher=[[IEEE]]}}</ref> 
the [[Free Haven Project]] distributed anonymous storage service,<ref>{{cite conference|title=Free Haven Project: Distributed anonymous storage service|first1=Roger|last1=Dingledine|first2=Michael|last2=Freedman|first3=David|last3=Molnar|year=2001|conference=Designing Privacy Enhancing Technologies|pages=67–95|publisher=Springer Berlin/Heidelberg|citeseerx = 10.1.1.420.478}}</ref> various attacks and vulnerabilities related to anonymity technologies,<ref>{{cite book|chapter=From a trickle to a flood: Active attacks on several As an advocate for strong privacy, Dingledine is frequently invited to speak about security and privacy, including at academic conferences,<ref name="cv"/> the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] (2014),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/cise/cns/watch/talks/dingledine.jsp|title=The Tor Project|author=Roger Dingledine|date=2014-01-14}}</ref> the [[National Security Agency|NSA]] (2007),<ref>{{cite news|title=Talk by Roger Dingledine of Torproject.org at the NSA|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|date=2013-10-04}}</ref> and periodic interviews.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.avast.com/cybersecai-connected-qa-with-roger-dingledine-avast|title=Roger Dingledine of Tor Project talks privacy and COVID-19 apps - A key figure at the heart of the debate around online privacy, Dingledine gives us his views on staying safe in the age of Covid|first=Malea|last=Lamb-Hall|date=2020-08-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.fosdem.org/2019/interviews/roger-dingledine/|publisher=FOSDEM 2019|title=Roger Dingledine - The Current and Future Tor Project. Updates from the Tor Project|date=2019-02-02}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Dingledine was named as one of the 2006 thirty-five [[Innovators Under 35]] by ''[[MIT Technology Review]]'', for his work on internet [[Anonymizer|anonymization]] technologies through the Tor Project.<ref name = MITTRinnovU3506>{{cite journal | author = MIT Tech Rev Staff | year = 2006 | title = Innovators Under 35: Roger Dingledine | journal = MIT Technology Review | issue = September/October | format = print and online | url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=583 | access-date=2016-12-31}}</ref> The ''Review'' described the importance of the work in this way:

{{quote| A dissident in China uses Web-based e-mail to contact a journalist in Canada. An intelligence agency wants to surveil a foreign website. Like every operation on the Internet, these activities leave tracks. Online anonymity measures provide a way around this problem; one of the most advanced is [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor]], or the [[Onion Router]]. / Computer scientist Roger Dingledine developed Tor ...<ref name = MITTRinnovU3506/>}}

In 2012, Dingledine and the other two initial developers of Tor, [[Nick Mathewson]] and [[Paul Syverson]], were recognized by [[Foreign Policy]] magazine as #78 in their top 100 global thinkers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2012/11/26/the-fp-top-100-global-thinkers-2/|title=The FP Top 100 Global Thinkers|date=2012-11-26|publisher=[[Foreign Policy]]}}</ref>

[[File:Roger Dingledine in 2023.jpg|thumb|right|Dingledine in 2023]]
==Media attention==
Dingledine has drawn attention after the [[leak of NSA documents]] by [[Edward Snowden]], and public disclosure of the rules guiding the operation of [[XKeyscore]], the NSA's collection system, given XKeyscore's targeting of Tor Project onion servers, including the one Dingledine runs at MIT, which serves a directory authority for the system, as well as being the base of operation of the [[Mixminion]] mail service, and host to various gaming and other websites (from which the [[NSA]] might be collecting IP addresses).<ref name = ZetterWired140703>{{cite magazine | author = Zetter, Kim | date = 2014-07-03 | title=The NSA Is Targeting Users of Privacy Services, Leaked Code Shows | magazine = Wired | format = print and online | url=https://www.wired.com/2014/07/nsa-targets-users-of-privacy-services/ | access-date = 2016-01-04 }}</ref>
<!--{{quote|The XKeyscore rules use features the NSA calls "appids," "fingerprints," and "microplugins," to identify and tag activity online. / Appids, the German publication notes, are unique identifiers that help the system sort and categorize data and user activity, such as an online search. The microplugins are possibly used to extract and store specific types of data. / The rules indicate that the NSA is specifically targeting the IP address of nine servers operated by key Tor volunteers in Germany, Sweden, Austria, the Netherlands and even the U.S. These servers are used by the Tor network as directory authorities. They generate, on an hourly basis, a directory of all the Tor nodes or relays on the Tor network, which change constantly as new servers are added by volunteers or taken out of the network. The Tor software consults these lists to direct traffic to the nodes. The XKeyscore system uses a fingerprint called "anonymizer/tor/node/authority" that targets any IP address that connects to the nine servers. / One of the servers is maintained by Sebastian Hahn, a 28-year-old a Tor volunteer and computer science student at the University of Erlangen. A German attorney told the media outlets that the targeting of Tor volunteers in Germany may violate restrictions against the US conducting secret intelligence activity against German citizens in Germany. / Another server is operated at MIT by Tor Project leader Roger Dingledine, an MIT alumnus. But in addition to serving as one of the Tor directory authorities, the server is also used to operate the MixMinion mail service and host a number of other web sites, including ones for online gaming libraries, which means the NSA may be collecting IP addresses for those users as well. <ref name = ZetterWired140703/>}}-->
